entries.ed556ff452219829c3c8cc1761432929eec4809a: Jdg 2:20-21 <hi type="italic">Chastisement of the Rebellious Nation</hi>. - Jdg 2:20, Jdg 2:21. On account of this idolatry, which was not only constantly repeated, but continued to grow worse and worse, the anger of the Lord burned so fiercely against Israel, that He determined to destroy no more of the nations which Joshua had left when he died, before the people that had broken His covenant. In order to set forth this divine purpose most distinctly, it is thrown into the form of a sentence uttered by God through the expression וגו ויּאמר. The Lord said, “Because this people has transgressed my covenant, ... I also will no longer keep my covenant promise (<reference osisRef="Exod.23.23">Exo 23:23</reference>, Exo 23:27., Exo 34:10.), and will no more drive out any of the remaining Canaanites before them” (see <reference osisRef="Josh.23.13">Jos 23:13</reference>).
entries.9c136adb4ff03ed5635518a68740dce0082eac31: Jdg 2:22 <div eID="gen3078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3079" type="x-p"/> The purpose of God in this resolution was “<hi type="italic">to prove Israel through them</hi> (the tribes that were not exterminated), <hi type="italic">whether they</hi> (the Israelites) <hi type="italic">would keep the way of the Lord to walk therein</hi> (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.8.2">Deu 8:2</reference>), <hi type="italic">as their fathers did keep it, or not</hi>.” נסּות למען is not dependent upon the verb עזב, as <hi type="italic">Studer</hi> supposes, which yields no fitting sense; nor can the clause be separated from the preceding one, as <hi type="italic">Bertheau</hi> suggests, and connected as a protasis with Jdg 2:23 (this would be a thoroughly unnatural construction, for which <reference osisRef="Isa.45.4">Isa 45:4</reference> does not furnish any true parallel); but the clause is attached in the simplest possible manner to the main thought in Jdg 2:20, Jdg 2:21, that is to say, to the words “<hi type="italic">and He said</hi>” in Jdg 2:20 : Jehovah said, i.e., resolved, that He would not exterminate the remaining nations any further, to tempt Israel through them. The plural בּם, in the place of the singular בּהּ, which the foregoing דּרך requires, is to be regarded as a <hi type="italic">constructio ad sensum</hi>, i.e., to be attributed to the fact, that keeping the way of God really consists in observing the commandments of God, and that this was the thought which floated before the writer’s mind. The thought expressed in this verse, that Jehovah would not exterminate the Canaanites before Israel any more, to try them whether they would keep His commandments, just as He had previously caused the people whom He brought out of Egypt to wander in the wilderness for forty years with the very same intention (<reference osisRef="Deut.8.2">Deu 8:2</reference>), is not at variance with the design of God, expressed in <reference osisRef="Exod.23.29-Exod.23.30">Exo 23:29-30</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Deut.7.22">Deu 7:22</reference>, not to exterminate the Canaanites all at once, lest the land should become waste, and the wild beasts multiply therein, nor yet with the motive assigned in Jdg 3:1-2. For the determination not to exterminate the Canaanite sin one single year, was a different thing from the purpose of God to suspend their gradual extermination altogether. The former purpose had immediate regard to the well-being of Israel; the latter, on the contrary, was primarily intended as a chastisement for its transgression of the covenants, although even this chastisement was intended to lead the rebellious nation to repentance, and promote its prosperity by a true conversion to the Lord. And the motive assigned in Jdg 2:2 is in perfect harmony with this intention, as our explanation of this passage will clearly show.
entries.0201ce9a336421dcd4be7001da31f7dc380b8e4d: Jdg 2:23 <div eID="gen3079" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3080" type="x-p"/> In consequence of this resolution, the Lord let these tribes (those mentioned in Jdg 3:3) remain at rest, i.e., quietly, in the land, without exterminating them rapidly. The expression מהר, hastily, quickly, i.e., according to the distinct words of the following clause, through and under Joshua, appears strange after what has gone before. For what is threatened in Jdg 2:21 is not the suspension of rapid extermination, but of any further extermination. This threat, therefore, is so far limited by the word “hastily,” as to signify that the Lord would not exterminate any more of these nations so long as Israel persisted in its idolatry. But as soon as and whenever Israel returned to the Lord its God in true repentance, to keep His covenant, the Lord would recall His threat, and let the promised extermination of the Canaanites go forward again. Had Israel not forsaken the Lord its God so soon after Joshua’s death, the Lord would have exterminated the Canaanites who were left in the land much sooner than He did, or have carried out their gradual extermination in a much shorter time than was actually the case, in consequence of the continual idolatry of the people.<hi type="italic">Nations which the Lord left in Canaan</hi>: with a repetition of the reason why this was done.  <chapter eID="Judg.2"/> <div eID="gen3080" type="x-p"/>
